statement: In college students, as described second-hand in a single-author narrative review of 62 published studies found up to February 2013, which pooled no data (Pearson, 2013), evidence is insufficient to say whether using more protective behavioural strategies (things people do just before, during or after drinking to limit their drinking or its harms, such as keeping track of drinks, alternating alcoholic and non-alcoholic drinks, eating, or using a designated driver), compared with using fewer, lowers drinking or alcohol-related problems. Students nearly always reported their strategies, drinking and problems themselves on questionnaires (at least 11 different ones), usually at one sitting and often for no stated period, so most links are associations reported by the same people, not predictions; the author estimates, without showing how, that 80% of the studies gave only cross-sectional data. By the author's account, nearly every study found that students who reported using more strategies also reported drinking less or having fewer problems, mostly as correlations whose sizes the review does not give; with one questionnaire, the link was negative when students rated how often they used strategies when they drank, but positive when they counted how many times they used them, a count that also rises with how often they drink (three studies by the author's team). In three studies, students reporting more strategies showed a weaker link between how much they drank and their problems. Over time the evidence was mixed: in a sample followed for a year after a peer intervention that showed no significant effect, correlations with later drinking were about as strong as those at the same time and changes in some kinds of strategy use went with less drinking or fewer problems, but correlations with later problems were weaker (3 of 9 not significant); in another study, strategy use rose after a brief intervention but the rise did not go with changes in drinking; and in women, strategy use was unrelated to drinking or problems at the same time point but went with fewer problems 4 months later. In two studies of day-by-day reports (a 15-day diary of 40 students, and a 7-day recall at one sitting around the 21st birthday), strategies about the way people drank went with less drinking on the days they were used, but people drank more on days they used limiting or stopping strategies, and drank more and had more problems on days with a designated driver or going home with a friend, which the author suggests reflects these strategies being planned for nights of heavy drinking. Students told to use more strategies reported using more but did not drink less (one experiment). In three trials of brief alcohol interventions, a rise in reported strategy use statistically mediated the interventions' effect on drinking or problems; in three others, the interventions did not change strategy use; none mainly targeted strategies. The author calls the trial and follow-up evidence mixed but ends by calling strategy use a promising way to reduce drinking and its harms. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
plain: In nearly every study of college students, those who said they used more safety habits when drinking also said they drank less or had fewer problems, but most studies asked about habits and drinking at the same time. Day by day, students drank more on days they had a designated driver or went home with a friend, which the review's author thinks happens because these are planned for nights of heavy drinking. Telling students to use more habits did not make them drink less in the one study that tried it, so whether the habits themselves lower drinking or harm is not known.
population: College students in 62 published quantitative studies found up to February 2013 (some samples appear in more than one study; countries not reported in the review), including incoming students, athletes, women and students sent to alcohol programmes, as summarized by one narrative review
exposure: Self-reported use of alcohol protective behavioural strategies, measured with at least 11 questionnaires in many versions (most often the Protective Behavioral Strategies Survey): strategies used just before, during or after drinking, such as setting a limit or leaving at a set time, alternating alcoholic and non-alcoholic drinks, drinking water, eating, avoiding drinking games or mixing types of alcohol, keeping track of drinks, using a designated driver or going home with a friend; 13 of the 62 studies also counted avoiding drinking altogether
comparator: Students reporting fewer strategies (between people, mostly cross-sectional); days without a given strategy (within people, two studies); control groups in trials of brief interventions, where strategy use was a measured mediator, not what was randomized; no instruction to use strategies (one experiment)
outcome: Self-reported alcohol use (amount, frequency, heavy drinking, estimated blood alcohol) and alcohol-related problems
magnitude: No pooled estimate; the review gives sizes for almost none of the strategy–outcome links. As described: nearly every study found that students reporting more strategies reported drinking less and/or fewer problems; with one questionnaire, correlations with drinking were negative on a how-often-when-drinking scale and positive on a scale counting the number of times strategies were used, which also counts drinking occasions (3 studies); a weaker drinking–problems link in 3 studies; in one sample followed for 12 months, prospective correlations with drinking similar to same-time ones, change in some kinds of strategy use predicting less drinking or fewer problems, and 3 of 9 prospective correlations with problems not significant; day by day (2 studies, one a 15-day diary of 40 students): less drinking on days with manner-of-drinking strategies, more on days with limiting or stopping strategies, more drinking and more problems on days with serious harm reduction strategies; mediation of intervention effects in 3 trials, no change in strategy use in 3 trials; no fall in drinking after an instruction to use more strategies (1 experiment). Studies with only cross-sectional data: 80% by the author's estimate (not derived; editors' rough count from the review's appendix, about 74% to 77%).

grade.reasoning: Mostly cross-sectional observational evidence starts low (in the trials the interventions were randomized, but strategy use was a measured mediator); rated down for risk of bias, inconsistency and indirectness, giving very low, the floor. statement: In an international online survey of people who had drunk ayahuasca (2017 to 2019; 6,877 self-selected respondents who had drunk with no more than two groups; Perkins et al., 2021), the setting of their last ceremony, as they described and rated it looking back, was associated with how much extreme fear they recalled and with difficulties afterwards, by small amounts. Of the 6,817 with a known setting, 52.1% had last drunk in an ayahuasca church (87% of them living in Brazil, and more than half having drunk over 200 times), 19.6% with traditional shamans and 28.3% in other settings; in these last two groups about two in three had drunk five times or fewer. Adjusted for age, sex, education, number of mental-health diagnoses, times drunk, years since the last drink, the three motivation scores and the other ceremony and support variables, each point higher on a 1-to-4 rating of support and safety (averages 3.4 to 3.9) went with less extreme fear or panic (−0.29 on a 0-to-10 scale, SE 0.07) and fewer difficulties in the weeks after (−0.13, SE 0.05); each point higher on a rating of the preparation offered (a chance to discuss one's history and concerns, and guidance on difficulties, before drinking) went with fewer later difficulties (−0.14, SE 0.03) but showed no detectable association with fear (−0.01, SE 0.04, p = 0.82). More fear went with more traditional practices (0.18 per practice, of up to 6), with drinking mostly in Amazonian countries other than Brazil (0.7), with therapeutic reasons for drinking (0.21 per reason) and with mental-health diagnoses (0.21 per diagnosis); less fear went with church features such as hymns or sermons (−0.38) and with each decade of age (−0.22). Fasting, offered at 35% of traditional settings, 26% of other settings and 2% of churches, showed no detectable difference in fear (−0.07 points on the 0-to-10 scale, 95% CI −0.29 to 0.15), later difficulties (−0.05, −0.21 to 0.11) or current distress (Kessler-10 −0.28, −0.69 to 0.13; editors' intervals): no difference was detected, which is not the same as showing there is none, since the fear interval runs from 0.29 points lower to 0.15 points higher. Fasting went with slightly higher ratings of mystical experience (1.7 points on a 9-to-90 scale) and of growth in well-being. Across the whole range of either rating, current distress differed by under 2 points on the 40-point Kessler scale (editors' arithmetic). Ratings and outcomes were reported by the same people at one sitting, on average 1.2 to 1.6 years after their last drink; the fear question did not say which session it meant, while the ceremony ratings concerned the last one; nothing was measured before ayahuasca, the amount and content of the brew were not recorded, no average or spread is given for the fear and difficulty measures, and the authors note that the sample may lean towards people with good experiences. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In one large survey, people who felt safe and supported at their last ayahuasca ceremony recalled a little less fear and fewer problems in the weeks after. Being offered a chance to talk things through beforehand went with fewer problems afterwards, but not with less fear, and fasting showed no detectable link with either. The same people rated the ceremony and their experience, looking back, and the differences were small.

exposure: Features of the last ceremony as the respondents described and rated them: church, traditional-shaman or other setting; support and safety; preparation offered; traditional or religious practices; fasting; country where they mostly drank
comparator: Respondents who rated or described their last ceremony differently, adjusted for age, sex, education, mental-health diagnoses, times drunk and years since the last drink
outcome: Extreme fear or panic during a session (0 to 10), difficulties in the weeks or months after, mystical-experience and growth ratings, and current distress (Kessler-10)

statement: In people who use benzodiazepines (prescribed, diverted, counterfeit or novel 'designer' benzodiazepines; most of the sources also involved opioids or stimulants), evidence is insufficient to say whether any harm reduction service or policy lowers harm. As described second-hand in a 2025 scoping review of 35 sources found up to July 2025, which mapped them without appraising them (Morrison et al., 2025), the approaches studied were drug checking (11 sources), prescribed benzodiazepines as treatment or safer supply (5), policies on scheduling, prescribing and surveillance (9) and approaches for particular groups (10); by the designs listed in the review's table, 17 were quantitative pilot, retrospective, cross-sectional or similar studies, 9 qualitative, 4 mixed-methods, 4 reviews and 1 a policy analysis, and none was a randomized trial. About half of the drug-checking sources (5 or 6 of 11 by the review's table, editors' count) tested how well drug-checking methods, mostly portable or point-of-care instruments checked against laboratory analysis, detect benzodiazepines: in 59 samples, a portable gas chromatography–mass spectrometer identified 36% of those containing etizolam (78% when etizolam was more than 3% of the sample by weight), against 9% with infrared spectroscopy. At one Canadian service, infrared analysis found alprazolam in 33 of 139 samples (23.7%) that people expected to be alprazolam (Xanax), and of 20 sent for confirmatory testing, 14 contained other active ingredients only. In a before-and-after pilot without a comparison group, among 68 of 103 women who do sex work and use drugs in Baltimore followed up a month after a fentanyl test-strip intervention, reported using alone fell from 96% to 68% and benzodiazepine use from 22% to 7%. In an observational study of 541 adults who use drugs in several US states, followed for 28 days, a positive fentanyl test-strip result went with reports of using smaller amounts, taking turns and keeping naloxone nearby, most strongly when benzodiazepines were tested; it relates test results to what people reported doing next, measures behaviour rather than harm and does not compare people offered drug checking with people who were not, and the review's text words this association as an effect. Prescribed benzodiazepines were described for 6 of 77 residents of COVID-19 isolation hotels, whose programme as a whole reported no overdoses (an evaluation the review cites as a preprint), and for more than 70 people experiencing homelessness in Dublin, from whom no feedback was collected; in one inner-London general practice, opioid substitution patients maintained on benzodiazepines (127 of 278) stayed in treatment longer than those prescribed none or only briefly (72 months against 34 and 51) and had a lower death rate in treatment than those prescribed none (1.31 against 1.79 per 100 patient-years; the review's table says the occasionally prescribed group had the lowest in-treatment death rate, without a figure), but a larger rise in deaths after leaving treatment, by figures the review reports inconsistently. After Australia moved alprazolam to a stricter schedule in 2014, four of five evaluations summarized in a 2021 review reported large falls in alprazolam use, along with falls in prescribing, dispensing, overdose deaths and poison-centre calls, while figures the authors cite from a letter, without definitions, show benzodiazepine overdose deaths overall rising from 160 in 2009 to 238 in 2015. After the United Kingdom rescheduled temazepam gel capsules, 100 people with long-term use of several drugs, in a qualitative study, described less injecting of capsules but continued injecting of tablets, higher prices, more acquisitive crime and substitution with flunitrazepam. The authors call drug checking the most widely reported approach, with consistently positive outcomes, and the results of prescribing and policy approaches mixed, without having appraised any source; they find harm reduction largely missing for people who are not seeking abstinence or treatment, and note that their search, built on the term harm reduction, may have missed studies. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Drug checking, prescribed benzos and stricter rules have all been tried for people who use benzos, but none has been tested in a way that shows whether it lowers harm. The review's authors call drug checking's results consistently positive, but those results are mostly about what tests detected and what people said they did afterwards. At one checking service, infrared testing found alprazolam, the drug in Xanax, in about 1 in 4 samples people thought were Xanax, and some testing methods often missed 'designer' benzos.
population: People who use benzodiazepines (prescribed, diverted, counterfeit or novel), in 35 sources gathered by one scoping review, most of which also involved opioids or stimulants: drug samples at checking services, clients of harm reduction services, women who do sex work, residents of COVID-19 isolation hotels, people in treatment, emergency-department and festival patients, forum posters and poison-centre callers

comparator: Mostly none; a few observational comparisons (patients maintained on benzodiazepines against others; positive against negative test results), before-and-after measurements without a control group, and one detection method against another (mostly portable or point-of-care methods against laboratory analysis)
outcome: Detection of benzodiazepines in drug samples; reported behaviour after testing; treatment retention and mortality; prescribing, use and deaths after policy changes; people's accounts
magnitude: No pooled estimates. Detection: portable gas chromatography–mass spectrometry 36% of etizolam-containing samples (78% above 3% by weight) against 9% with infrared (59 samples); a miniature mass spectrometer quantified etizolam in 11 of 15 samples that strips and/or infrared had failed to detect or quantify. Expected alprazolam: 33 of 139 (23.7%) by infrared; of 20 confirmed, 2 alprazolam alone, 4 alprazolam with other ingredients, 14 other ingredients only. Toronto: of 555 samples, 15 were expected to be benzodiazepines, and benzodiazepine-type drugs were found in 116; benzodiazepine-type drugs present in 24 (41%) of samples linked to a negative effect (presence, not cause). After test strips (pilot, 68 of 103 followed up): using alone 96% to 68%, benzodiazepine use 22% to 7%; 69% reported a harm reduction behaviour. Prescribed benzodiazepines: 6 of 77 hotel residents (cited from a preprint); more than 70 people in Dublin. Poison-centre line: safety information to 6635 of 17,616 callers (37.7%), no outcome evaluation.

statement: In people who use benzodiazepines, evidence is insufficient to say whether anything they do themselves before or during use lowers harm: as described second-hand in a 2025 scoping review of 35 sources that did not appraise them (Morrison et al., 2025), no source compared people who used such a practice with people who did not, and none measured harm as an outcome of a practice. Practices appear as people's accounts, researchers' recommendations and reports of behaviour after drug checking: in a study of a Swedish online drug forum about flubromazolam (122 in the review's table), posters described limiting their own access to the drug while intoxicated, staying at home, limiting how often they used, avoiding alcohol at the same time and comparing vendors and batches; in British Columbia during COVID-19, women and gender-diverse people who use drugs (45, in a qualitative study) formed informal peer networks to check on one another because of benzodiazepine contamination and the risk of sexual assault; in an ethnography in Melbourne, one participant described using temazepam at home to avoid losing money or drugs, or being arrested, while sedated; and the authors of a survey of 252 people who inject drugs in Bangkok called for education against injecting alone. Numbers come only from two drug-checking studies, and they describe behaviour, not harm: in a before-and-after pilot without a comparison group, in which 103 women who do sex work and use drugs in Baltimore received fentanyl test strips, 69% of the 68 followed up a month later reported doing something to lower harm after a result, such as asking someone to check on them, and reported using alone fell from 96% to 68%; and in an observational study of 541 adults who use drugs in several US states, a positive fentanyl test-strip result went, over 28 days, with reports of using smaller amounts, taking turns and keeping naloxone nearby, most strongly when benzodiazepines were tested (an association in the review's table, which its text words as a result of the strip). The review searched on terms such as harm reduction and did not cover peer-led resources, so practices described elsewhere may be missing; its authors find harm reduction largely absent for people who are not seeking abstinence or treatment. statement: As described in one scoping review (Kheirkhah et al., 2024; searched to December 2023; the included studies were not appraised, so its figures are second-hand), evidence is insufficient to say whether music changes how a ketamine or esketamine session goes. The review found 14 studies of music with ketamine, all in patients in clinical or trial settings. In nine, ketamine was given with other sedatives or painkillers, during procedures or, in one study, air medical transport; in most of them music went with less sedation or drug use and lower anxiety, pain or fear, but one trial found no effect on emergence reactions and another found more dreams or emergence reactions with music, though no unpleasant dreams, against 10 controls with unpleasant dreams. Of the five studies of ketamine or esketamine alone, only one compared people who listened with people who heard nothing: in 46 children having heart catheterization under ketamine anaesthesia, the 23 who heard recordings of their mothers' voices (musical in 12 of them) had less anxiety before the procedure and fewer emergence reactions than 23 who wore headphones with no recording. The other four were case reports and interview studies without such a comparison: a woman on esketamine nasal spray found that music of her choice helped with dissociation, confusion and anxiety; two patients with bipolar depression tolerated dissociation better with preferred music in later infusions, which may reflect getting used to the infusions; in 12 people given ketamine in a trial for alcohol use disorder, everyone who listened to music heard it distorted in speed and pitch, felt as good or bad depending on their state; and in 17 people on oral esketamine for depression, music was described as blocking distractions and helping inner exploration, but some felt it kept them tied to the outside world and one stopped using it. Up to its search, the review found no study comparing music with no music during ketamine or esketamine treatment for depression, and its own limitations say no conclusions can be drawn; a randomized clinical trial of music with ketamine for depression published after that search (Greenway et al., 2024) has not yet been read for this answer. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: A review found 14 studies of music with ketamine, all with patients. Only one study of ketamine alone compared listening with silence: children who heard their mother's voice were less anxious. The review, searched to the end of 2023, found no study comparing music with no music during ketamine treatment for depression, so it is not known whether music helps; a trial published in 2024 has not been read here yet.

statement: In 213 healthy volunteers aged 25 to 64 (108 women) who took LSD mostly lying in bed in a quiet hospital room with one investigator present (some sessions included an MRI scan), and placebo on another day in eight of the nine studies (nine double-blind crossover studies pooled by the Basel laboratory that ran them, 297 LSD sessions; one dose by mouth per session, 25 to 200 micrograms, as study conditions; Vizeli et al., 2024), the dose given was the strongest predictor of almost every effect compared with placebo, and characteristics measured before the dose were also associated with the response at a given dose: higher well-being rated just before, with stronger subjective effects in general, by the Discussion's summary (it was significantly associated with every self-rated scale, the anxiety-type scales included, except a bad drug effect and two others; the direction scale by scale is shown only in a figure not read); anxiety rated just before, with more anxiety during the session; openness, with more mystical-type and oceanic ratings; extraversion, with more visual and auditory changes; more previous hallucinogen experience, with a smaller overall altered state and less anxious ego dissolution; and genetically lower activity of the liver enzyme CYP2D6, with higher blood levels of LSD and more anxious ego dissolution. Neuroticism, agreeableness and conscientiousness showed no significant association with any effect. Older age went with more, and higher body weight with less, bad drug effect, and women had smaller increases than men in four positive ratings and in body temperature; women's slightly less positive ratings were not significant when one dose per study was analysed (the text does not say whether the temperature difference held), and the abstract's statement that sex and body weight had no significant influence does not match the main results. The text gives the direction and significance of each association after correction for 551 tests but no sizes, which are only in a figure and a supplement not read here, so how much any characteristic other than dose matters cannot be said; bad drug effects were generally small. Expectations were not among the 19 predictors, and the setting barely varied. Genes for the CYP2D6 enzyme and earlier hallucinogen use went with feeling more or less from the same amount; earlier use was compared between people, so it cannot show that use itself changed the response. Everyone took one fixed dose per session, so what happens when someone who feels little takes more was not tested. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In laboratory studies of healthy adults, the LSD dose was linked most closely to how strong the effects were. People who felt well just before had stronger effects, people who felt anxious had more anxiety, open personalities had more mystical feelings, and people who had used hallucinogens more often had a smaller overall effect. The paper gives the direction of each link but not its size. Everyone took one fixed dose per session, so what happens when someone who feels little takes more was not tested.

comparator: Volunteers with lower or higher values of each characteristic, at a given dose (placebo sessions in the same people in eight of nine studies)
outcome: Self-rated effects relative to placebo (visual analogue scales, 5D-ASC, MEQ30), blood pressure, heart rate, body temperature and blood LSD level
magnitude: Directions and corrected significance only; no sizes in the text. Dose strongest for every effect except body temperature (selected by LASSO for all 29 responses, largest for 21). statement: In 194 healthy, screened volunteers aged 18 to 45, four in five new to MDMA, who took MDMA by mouth lying in a quiet hospital ward in Basel, with a placebo on another day (10 double-blind crossover studies pooled by the laboratory that ran them; a single dose in each analysed session, 125 mg for 164 people and 75 mg for 30, the same for women and men, as study conditions; 112 of them also took MDMA in another session after a medicine given first, which was not analysed; Studerus et al., 2021), the amount taken per kilogram of body weight and the blood level went most with how strongly the effects were felt, as the volunteers rated them. Without adjustment, the blood level was associated with the rating of any drug effect (standardized beta 0.48), and in penalized models dose per kilogram was selected for 21 of 25 effects and ranked first for 12, among them any drug effect, good drug effect, high mood, feeling stimulated and liking, but mattered less for unpleasant or anxious reactions. At the same dose per kilogram, genetically lower activity of the liver enzyme CYP2D6 went with a higher blood level (beta −0.19), older age with a smaller rise in heart rate (−0.27), higher openness with more closeness to others (0.28) and oceanic boundlessness (0.22), higher neuroticism (rated at screening) and trait anxiety with more dread of ego dissolution (0.32 each) and impaired control (0.26 each), and a more anxious-depressed or introverted mood just before the dose with more anxiety (0.25 and 0.23); oceanic boundlessness, dread of ego dissolution, impaired control and anxiety were rated on a questionnaire at the end of the session, looking back over it. Each of these associations survived correction for multiple testing and was modest, explaining 5 to 12% of the variation (semi-partial R2). For a rating of a bad drug effect, older age, trait anxiety and anxious-depressed mood before the dose ranked highest in the penalized models, but the association with age did not survive correction for multiple testing in the main models. Women and men did not differ significantly once dose per kilogram was allowed for; because everyone took a fixed amount and women weighed less, women received more per kilogram, so sex and dose per kilogram went together and cannot be cleanly separated in these data (dose per kilogram varied from 0.8 to 2.7 mg/kg across the volunteers). The authors note that this does not confirm earlier studies that found differences between women and men even after adjusting for body weight, and they cite others, among them an earlier report on safety data from these studies (Vizeli and Liechti, 2017), suggesting that women may be more prone to unpleasant effects, while a three-laboratory study of 220 people detected no differences between women and men. Previous MDMA use showed no association, but no one had used it more than five times before the study. Expectations were not among the measures, and the setting, highly standardized, could not be studied. So differences between bodies went with feeling more or less from the same amount: at a fixed amount a lighter body meant more per kilogram, which went with stronger effects, and genetically lower enzyme activity went with a higher blood level; each analysed session had one fixed dose, so what happens when someone who feels little takes more was not tested here (controlled studies of a second dose are covered in a separate answer). Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In laboratory studies of healthy young adults, how much MDMA they got for their body weight, and how much reached the blood, went most with how strongly they felt it. Women and men did not clearly differ once body weight was allowed for, although an earlier report from the same laboratory suggested women may feel more unpleasant effects. Each session had one fixed amount, so what happens when someone who feels little takes more was not tested.

statement: In clients of 27 harm reduction supply sites across British Columbia, Canada, surveyed in 2018 (414 people aged 19 or older who had used illicit drugs in the past 6 months, recruited by convenience at the sites), 314 (75.8%; editors' 95% CI 71.5% to 79.7%) said they had used drugs alone at least once in the past 7 days, and 198 (47.8%) more than a quarter of the time, answering one question that did not define alone (Papamihali et al., 2020). Offered a short list of reasons, with more than one allowed, the 314 most often chose that it is more convenient and comfortable to use at home (139, 44.3%; 52.7% of the 264 who gave a reason, editors' calculation), then not wanting others to know (44, 14.0%; more often under age 50 than at 50 or older, 16.9% against 5.3%) and that it is safer to be alone (30, 9.6%). Two more reasons were not on the list but were coded by the authors from written answers: having no one to use with (37, 11.7%) and not wanting to share or it being cheaper (27, 8.6%); because they could be given only in writing, their shares cannot be ranked against the listed options and may be undercounts. Written answers also included having no access to an overdose prevention site and not being allowed to use in a transition home. People who used alone more often had no regular housing (37.6% against 24.0% of those who did not use alone; adjusted odds ratio 2.27, 95% CI 1.20 to 4.27, in 306 people with complete answers) and more often had used crack or cocaine in the past week (41.4% against 26.0%; 2.10, 1.15 to 3.82). They also more often reported an opioid or stimulant overdose in the past 6 months (22.9% against 15.0%), but not significantly after adjustment (1.71, 0.79 to 3.69); both were reported by the same people at one sitting, so this is an association, not a prediction, and the survey cannot say whether using alone changes the risk of overdose. Coroners' reports cited in the paper's background, not data of this study, found that 69% of people who died of an overdose in British Columbia in 2016–2017 were using alone and that in 2019 the place of injury was a private residence for more than half of illicit drug overdose deaths; the paper does not say how these deaths were defined or how using alone was established. People already in contact with services were surveyed, so the figures may not hold for people who use drugs and do not attend these sites. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In a 2018 survey at 27 harm reduction sites in British Columbia, Canada, about 3 in 4 people had used drugs alone at least once in the past week. The survey could not show whether using alone changes the risk of overdose, but coroners' reports it cites found that about 7 in 10 people who died of an overdose in the province in 2016 and 2017 were using alone.

statement: In adults who have used classic psychedelics, evidence is insufficient to say whether anything people do during a difficult experience makes it shorter or easier: no study read here tested a way of coping, and what is known is what people say helped, looking back. Two independent surveys agree only that a calming or accepting response (trying to calm the mind; letting go or accepting the experience) was the one most often named as helpful; their lists and questions differed, so their percentages cannot be compared. In a self-selected online survey of 529 people recalling a challenging experience with a classic psychedelic or an analogue (psilocybin, ayahuasca, LSD, DMT or mescaline; use combined with non-classic drugs such as MDMA or ketamine was allowed) (Wood et al., 2024), the responses, of 26 listed, most often tried and judged helpful were letting go, accepting or surrendering (84.5%), observing the mind without fighting it (77.3%) and closing the eyes or lying or sitting down (73.9%); the least often were directing anger at the experience (9.4%), trying to sleep (9.7%), telling it to stop (10.6%) and taking another drug or alcohol (12.1%). People who judged more of the 11 responses that the authors grouped as acceptance and reappraisal helpful rated their emotional breakthrough higher (r = 0.50), but that group also includes breathing, closing the eyes, questioning the experience, telling it to stop and directing anger at it; both were rated at one sitting, sometimes years later, and judging a response helpful may itself reflect how the experience ended. Sixteen people who had attended psilocybin retreats, chosen because their difficult ceremonies had been followed by personal change, wrote of breathing on purpose, opening their eyes and moving, engaging with the surroundings, asking for help, and facilitators' touch, listening, reassurance and reminders to breathe, among other responses. In a US online panel, 613 adults who had used a classic psychedelic, including 362 who said they had never had a challenging experience, ticked what had helped during their most challenging one: trying to calm the mind 257 (41.9%), changing location 168 (27.4%), asking a friend for help 124 (20.2%), changing the people around 124 (20.2%), smoking cannabis 113 (18.4%) and changing the music 99 (16.2%); fewer ticked drinking alcohol (54, 8.8%) or taking another drug (22, 3.6%) (Simonsson et al., 2023). No study tested any of these responses, including taking cannabis, alcohol or another drug, which in the other survey was among the responses least often judged helpful (12.1%). As summarized second-hand in a mini review (Piercey et al., 2024), 91% of respondents to an earlier survey of difficult experiences with psilocybin mushrooms used at least one such strategy and rated them only modestly effective, and 65.9% of surveyed callers to a psychedelic peer-support phone line (the drugs they had taken are not stated) said it helped ease their distress. None of these studies compared people who did something with people who did not. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: Looking back, people most often said that letting go, watching their thoughts without fighting them, calming the mind, or closing their eyes and lying down helped during a difficult trip; moving somewhere else or asking a friend also came up. None of the studies tested whether any of these actually helps: no study compared people who did them with people who did not.

statement: In adults who planned, on their own initiative, to take a classic psychedelic, a better state of mind measured before the drug is associated with a less challenging experience, and in laboratory LSD sessions mood and personality measured before the dose were associated with how the session went; many of the larger associations reported come from people recalling afterwards how they had felt. In the only prospective study outside a laboratory among these sources (Haijen et al., 2018; self-selected adults who answered online surveys; of the 379 who reported back, 48% took LSD or 1P-LSD, 29% psilocybin and 11% ayahuasca), feeling comfortable, open, well prepared, not anxious and in a good mood, rated by the participants within the day before ('set'), went with lower Challenging Experience Questionnaire scores they gave about a day after (standardized beta −0.32, SE 0.07; moderate in the editors' terms), as did recreational or social intentions rated a week before (−0.22; small). Strong expectations and a clear intention went with higher mystical-type (0.18) and visual (0.16) scores but not clearly with challenge, and set was unrelated to mystical-type scores. The trait absorption went with more intense experiences of every kind, challenging (0.22) as well as mystical-type (0.35), while trait anxiety, openness, emotional stability, suggestibility and the number of earlier psychedelic experiences showed no statistically significant association with any of them in this model of about 198 people. The sample shrank from 654 a week before to about 198 in this analysis (editors' inference), and the predictors were adjusted for one another and for an amount the participants estimated after the experience, not for the drug taken or psychiatric history. Average well-being rose from 49.0 before to 52.6 two weeks after, with no comparison group and fewer than half the sample remaining, and mystical-type scores no longer predicted it once traits, intentions, set and setting were in the model. In healthy volunteers given LSD, mostly lying in bed in a quiet hospital room and mostly with a placebo session for comparison (nine Basel laboratory studies, 213 people; Vizeli et al., 2024), higher well-being rated on a mood questionnaire before the dose went with stronger effects on every self-rated scale except a rating of a bad drug effect and two others, the anxiety scales included, so in these sessions a better mood went with a stronger experience rather than a less challenging one; anxiety rated before the dose went with more anxiety during the session, and openness with more mystical-type ratings, all at a given dose; the text gives no sizes. In two retrospective studies of people who had used psilocybin, as summarized by a systematic review the editors rate critically low (Aday et al., 2021), states recalled after the experience were associated with it; in the one for which the review gives figures (143 people), surrender correlated with mystical-type experience (r = 0.72) and preoccupation and confusion with dread (0.64 and 0.58). In a US online panel, people who blamed a negative mindset for their most challenging experience rated it as more challenging (beta 0.14) and more often reported thoughts or attempts to hurt themselves or others afterwards (odds ratio 4.56, 95% CI 2.10 to 9.94, adjusted only for the other circumstances respondents could tick; 41 of the 613 reported any; Simonsson et al., 2023). Such recalled states are associations reported by the same people at the same sitting, not predictors. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: People who felt calm, open and ready the day before a trip they had planned rated it as less difficult. In laboratory LSD sessions, feeling anxious beforehand went with more anxiety, while feeling well went with stronger effects overall, not easier ones. These links come from watching, not testing, and many people dropped out of the study outside the laboratory. Studies in which people recalled their mood afterwards found bigger links, but memories can be coloured by how the trip went.

exposure: State of mind, intentions and traits measured before the drug (set within a day before; intentions and traits a week before; mood before a laboratory dose, personality at screening), and, in retrospective studies, states recalled afterwards
comparator: People with lower or higher scores on each measure within the same study; no study compared people helped to prepare with people who were not
outcome: How challenging, mystical-type or intense the experience was, self-rated (Challenging Experience Questionnaire, Mystical Experience Questionnaire, 5D-ASC, visual analogue scales), and well-being in the following weeks
magnitude: Haijen et al. risk_of_bias.note: The prospective study is at high risk of bias (drug type, psychiatric history and other drugs not adjusted; the amount estimated after the experience; about 70% of the baseline sample not in the analysis; when the day-before survey was completed could not be confirmed, and it could be filled in on paper and entered later), the laboratory analysis has some concerns (each predictor adjusted for dose only; no sizes in the text), and the recalled-state findings are at very high risk (attributions made at the same sitting as the outcome) and are worded only as associations (cards sc_haijen_2018, sc_vizeli_2024, sc_aday_2021, sc_simonsson_2023).

inconsistency.note: More anxiety, alone or within a worse overall state of mind, measured before the drug went with a more anxious or more challenging experience in both the naturalistic and the laboratory source. In the laboratory a better general mood went with stronger effects overall, the anxiety scales included by the text, rather than with a less challenging session; that is a different mood scale and outcome from the naturalistic study's set component, so the claim states it instead of rating it as inconsistency (the certainty would stay very low either way). Absorption's link with mystical and challenging experience alike is reported, not a conflict.

indirectness.note: Worded for the populations studied (self-selected, mostly experienced people planning their own use; screened laboratory volunteers).

imprecision.note: The main prospective coefficient has a standard error of 0.07; for the laboratory analysis only directions are claimed.

publication_bias.note: The review admitted only predictors reported as significant, a file-drawer problem its authors name; the primary studies are cited directly and the review's figures are labelled as summarized.

grade.reasoning: Predictor studies start low, even inside randomized laboratory studies, because the predictors were not randomized; down one for risk of bias, giving very low. Status replicated, for the direction only: more anxiety beforehand, alone or within a worse overall state of mind, went with a more anxious or more challenging experience in two independent sources measured before the drug, one prospective and naturalistic (Imperial College London, the set component) and one laboratory (Basel, pre-dose anxiety), with different questionnaires, so it is a conceptual replication; recalled attributions in an independent panel (Simonsson et al.) point the same way. That a better mood goes with an easier experience rests on the naturalistic study alone: in the laboratory a better mood went with stronger effects overall. The other predictors rest on single studies or on states recalled afterwards. The review (Aday et al., 2021) is used only for what it adds (the retrospective Russ studies and the tabulation of absorption), since its Table 1 misprints the sign for set.

statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether music played during a psychedelic session changes how it goes or what follows: no study read here compared sessions with and without music, or with different music. In an open-label trial of psilocybin for treatment-resistant depression (Kaelen et al., 2018), 19 patients each had two psilocybin sessions lying with eye-shades in a furnished room in a clinical research facility, with two therapists and one standard playlist (one patient who strongly disliked it in the first session heard a different playlist in the second). In interviews a week after the second session, 18 of 19 described welcome influences of the music (it intensified the experience for 17, guided 15 and calmed 10) and 10 of 19 unwelcome ones (it intensified feelings they did not want, or felt uncomfortable or irritating); 9 resisted where the music was taking them and 6 felt misguided by it, mostly by music that clashed with what they were going through. Four researchers' ratings of how much each patient had liked the music, resonated with it and been open to it, made from those interviews, correlated with the fall in self-rated depression recorded at the same time point, a week after the second session (liking r = 0.60, 95% CI 0.20 to 0.83; resonance 0.59, 0.19 to 0.82; openness 0.57, 0.16 to 0.81; editors' intervals), while the patients' own rating of how intense the drug had been did not (r = 0.004, −0.45 to 0.46). The music was rated after any improvement had happened, at the same time point, so patients who felt better may have described it more warmly; the three ratings were so closely related (r 0.90 to 0.96) that they probably measure one thing, agreement between the raters averaged r = 0.6 (the authors call this good), nothing was adjusted, and the authors say that without a placebo condition causal inferences are problematic. In a US online panel of 613 adults who had used a classic psychedelic, 30 (4.9%) named disagreeable music among the things associated with their most challenging experience; naming it was not associated with how challenging they rated the experience (standardized beta 0.05, p = 0.19) nor, with an interval too wide to tell, with thoughts or attempts to hurt themselves or others in the days or weeks after (odds ratio 2.67, 95% CI 0.87 to 8.21, with the other listed factors entered together), and 99 (16.2%) ticked changing the music among actions that had helped during it (Simonsson et al., 2023). Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In one small study of 19 patients given psilocybin in a clinic, almost all said the music helped at times, and about half said it sometimes made things harder. Patients who spoke more warmly about the music had a bigger drop in depression, but both were measured at the same time, a week later, so feeling better may have coloured how they described the music. None of the studies we read compared sessions with and without music.

statement: In people who use classic psychedelics, feeling safe and supported is associated with fewer reported difficulties in retrospective surveys, while the only prospective study among these sources found only a weak, uncertain link for the place and the people. In that study (Haijen et al., 2018; about 198 self-selected adults who planned an experience on their own initiative), a good feeling about the people who would be present and about the place, rated within the day before, went with slightly lower Challenging Experience Questionnaire scores rated about a day after (standardized beta −0.14, p = 0.070, not statistically significant), and with slightly higher well-being two weeks later (1.2 points on the well-being scale per standard deviation of the rating, p = 0.037, one of many coefficients in a model without correction for multiple tests; not significant at four weeks, p = 0.077); a retreat or a setting designed for therapy, reported afterwards in two yes-or-no questions that the authors combined into one variable, showed no statistically significant association with any acute measure (0.02), and the authors note that the term was not defined for participants. In an international online survey of 6,877 self-selected people who had drunk ayahuasca, each point higher on a 1-to-4 rating of support and safety at their last ceremony went with 0.29 points less extreme fear or panic on a 0-to-10 scale (95% CI 0.15 to 0.43, editors' calculation), slightly fewer difficulties in the weeks after, and current distress lower by 0.62 points on the 40-point Kessler scale, under 2 points across the whole rating (editors' arithmetic), after adjustment for age, sex, education, mental-health diagnoses, times drunk and years since the last drink and for the motivation, ceremony and other support variables; the ratings were made looking back by the same people, and averaged near the top of the scale (Perkins et al., 2021). Among 613 US adults in an online panel who had used a classic psychedelic, those who blamed a lack of psychological support for their most challenging experience rated it as more challenging (beta 0.25) and more often reported thoughts or attempts to hurt themselves or others in the days or weeks after (odds ratio 2.85, 95% CI 1.27 to 6.42, adjusted only for the other circumstances respondents could tick; 41 of the 613 reported any); blaming a disagreeable physical environment went with a smaller difference in challenge (0.09) and no detectable difference in harm thoughts, and blaming the people around with no statistically significant difference in either (odds ratio for harm thoughts 0.33, 0.11 to 1.01, p = 0.051, lower if anything) (Simonsson et al., 2023). Among 163 experienced people recalling two experiences, mostly at home or at a friend's house, those whose experience was at a party, club or festival (24 first and 12 most recent experiences) had higher average challenge scores than the rest (19 against 17 and 31 against 16 per cent of the maximum), a comparison the authors did not test (Palmer and Maynard, 2022). No study compared settings by design. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
plain: In surveys, people who felt safe and supported during a trip reported a little less fear and fewer difficulties, but they rated both afterwards. The only study among these that asked people beforehand found only a weak, uncertain link between feeling good about the place and the people and how the trip went, and no detectable difference for retreats or settings designed for therapy. No study put people in different settings on purpose to compare them.
population: People who use classic psychedelics outside laboratories: adults who planned an experience on their own initiative (one prospective study), people who drink ayahuasca (one international survey), a US online panel and a self-selected survey of experienced people
exposure: The place and the people: feelings about the setting rated the day before; a retreat or therapeutic setting; support and safety at an ayahuasca ceremony rated afterwards; lack of support, a disagreeable place or disagreeable company blamed for the most challenging experience; party, club or festival settings
comparator: People who rated the setting less favourably, did not blame it, or used elsewhere, within each study
outcome: Challenging experience (Challenging Experience Questionnaire), extreme fear or panic, difficulties in the weeks after, thoughts or attempts to hurt oneself or others, and current distress (Kessler-10)
magnitude: Haijen et al. Perkins et al. risk_of_bias.note: Retrospective ratings or attributions made by the same people at the same sitting as the outcome, in self-selected samples, with little or no adjustment (very high risk: sc_perkins_2021, sc_simonsson_2023, sc_palmer_2022); the prospective study is at high risk (confounding, heavy attrition) and its retreat item was undefined (sc_haijen_2018).

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; down two for risk of bias and one for inconsistency, giving very low (the floor). Status mixed: four independent studies; support and safety went with fewer difficulties in two retrospective surveys (Perkins et al.; the no-support attribution in Simonsson et al.) and the untested party comparison points the same way, but blaming the people around showed no such link, and the one prospective study found only a non-significant trend for its setting rating (and a weak link with well-being two weeks later) and no association for a retreat or therapeutic setting; recall at the same sitting may explain part of the difference, but no study has shown that it does.
